lede: The Qurʾan’s last surah is a prayer for protection against the enemy that is hardest to see, because it speaks in one’s own voice. Against that single danger it calls on Allah by three names.

names.name: al-Nās
names.note: After the word that ends five of its six ayat. The Prophet ﷺ called it by its opening: Qul aʿūdhu bi-rabbi l-nās.

names.name: al-Muʿawwidhatān
names.note: The name it shares with al-Falaq.

revelation.detail: It goes with al-Falaq: the two came down together and the same two views are reported, both from Ibn ʿAbbās — that it is Madinan, in the report of Abū Ṣāliḥ, and that it is Makkan, in another. Al-Qurṭubī says simply that it is like al-Falaq, being one of the two surahs of refuge. The muṣḥaf heads it Makkan.
revelation.when: With al-Falaq: Makkah on one view, Madinah on the other

evidence.quote: وَفِيها قَوْلانِ. أحَدُهُما: أنَّها مَدَنِيَّةٌ، رَواهُ أبُو صالِحٍ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ. والثّانِي: أنَّها مَكِّيَّةٌ

setting: What is reported of al-Falaq’s setting is reported of this surah too; they were sent down as a pair, and the Prophet ﷺ announced them together: “Ayat have been sent down tonight the like of which has never been seen.”

The two divide the field between them. Al-Falaq asks protection from what happens to a person — things done by others, which may harm his body or his life but do not make him guilty of anything. Al-Nās asks protection from the one harm that does: the prompting to do wrong himself. That is why, Ibn al-Qayyim observes, the balance is reversed. There, one name of Allah stands against four evils. Here, three names — Lord, King, God — stand against one.

The one is al-waswās al-khannās: the whisperer who draws back. The early commentators explained the second word from Ibn ʿAbbās: the devil crouches over the heart of the son of Ādam; when he is heedless, it whispers, and when he remembers Allah, it withdraws.
aim: To hold fast to Allah and take shelter in Him from the evil of the devil and his whispering, and from the evils that are hidden.

outline.title: With Whom
outline.summary: Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, the God of mankind. He who made and sustains them, He who rules them, and He alone whom they are to worship: the three together leave no one else to turn to.

outline.title: From what
outline.summary: From the evil of the whisperer who withdraws, who whispers into the breasts of mankind — from among jinn and men. The whisperer is not only a devil unseen; a human companion can do the same work.

keyAyah.why: The one danger the surah was sent against, named so that it can be recognised.

virtues.text: “Have you not seen the ayat that were sent down tonight, the like of which has never been seen? ‘Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak’ and ‘Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind’.”

Each night when the Prophet ﷺ went to his bed he would bring his palms together, blow into them and recite into them “Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad”, “Qul aʿūdhu bi-rabbi l-falaq” and “Qul aʿūdhu bi-rabbi l-nās”, then wipe with them as much of his body as he could, beginning with his head and face and the front of his body. He would do that three times.
“Say ‘Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad’ and the two surahs of refuge three times when evening comes and when morning comes: they will suffice you against everything.”
virtues.grade: Ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb, said al-Tirmidhī; ḥasan according to al-Albānī

before: Al-Falaq sought refuge from four evils that come from outside, by one of Allah’s attributes. Al-Nās seeks refuge from one that works within, by three.

notable.label: Lord, King and God of mankind

sources: Ibn al-Qayyim, on the two surahs of refuge
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī
